# Cyrillic Alphabet

Russian uses the Cyrillic alphabet, which has 33 letters. Some look like Latin letters and sound the same (А, К, М), some look familiar but sound different (Р = "r", Н = "n", В = "v"), and others are entirely new (Ж, Щ, Ы).

## Core Vocabulary

| Cyrillic | romanization | English |
|----------|--------------|---------|
| А а | a | "a" as in father |
| Б б | b | "b" as in book |
| В в | v | "v" as in vine |
| Г г | g | "g" as in go |
| Д д | d | "d" as in dog |
| Е е | ye/e | "ye" as in yes |
| Ё ё | yo | "yo" as in yore |
| Ж ж | zh | "s" in pleasure |
| З з | z | "z" as in zoo |
| И и | i | "ee" as in see |
| Й й | y | "y" as in boy |
| К к | k | "k" as in kite |
| Л л | l | "l" as in lamp |
| М м | m | "m" as in moon |
| Н н | n | "n" as in nose |
| О о | o | "o" as in more |
| П п | p | "p" as in pen |
| Р р | r | rolled "r" |
| С с | s | "s" as in sun |
| Т т | t | "t" as in top |
| У у | u | "oo" as in boot |
| Ф ф | f | "f" as in fish |
| Х х | kh | "ch" as in Bach |
| Ц ц | ts | "ts" as in cats |
| Ч ч | ch | "ch" as in chair |
| Ш ш | sh | "sh" as in shoe |
| Щ щ | shch | softer, longer "sh" |
| Ъ ъ | (hard sign) | silent, hardens preceding consonant |
| Ы ы | y | guttural "i", no English equivalent |
| Ь ь | (soft sign) | silent, softens preceding consonant |
| Э э | e | "e" as in echo |
| Ю ю | yu | "yu" as in use |
| Я я | ya | "ya" as in yard |

## Example Sentences

- **мама** (mama) — mom
- **папа** (papa) — dad
- **дом** (dom) — house
- **кот** (kot) — cat
- **молоко** (moloko) — milk
- **спасибо** (spasibo) — thank you
- **Россия** (Rossiya) — Russia
- **Москва** (Moskva) — Moscow

## Script Notes

- "False friends": Russian Р = "r", С = "s", Н = "n", В = "v", У = "u", Х = "kh". Don't read them like Latin letters.
- Е, Ё, Ю, Я are "iotated" vowels: they carry a /y/ sound at the start of a word or after a vowel (Юра = "Yura"), and palatalize the preceding consonant elsewhere.
- Ъ (hard sign) and Ь (soft sign) are never pronounced alone. Ь softens the consonant before it: мать (mat') = "mother".
- Cyrillic has italic and cursive forms that differ from print: italic т looks like "m", italic д like "g". Don't be alarmed.

## Common Mistakes

- Pronouncing В as English "B" — it's "V".
- Treating Н as English "H" — it's "N".
- Skipping the soft/hard sign distinction.
- Mixing up Ш (sh) and Щ (shch).

## Try It Yourself

1. Write your name in Cyrillic.
2. Read aloud: мама, папа, дом, кот, молоко.
3. Decode: МОСКВА, РОССИЯ, ВОДКА, КОФЕ.
4. Find the four "false-friend" letters in your name's Russian transliteration.

## Next Steps

Once you can read Cyrillic letter-by-letter, move on to pronunciation rules — Russian spelling is fairly phonetic, but stress and vowel reduction will change how letters sound.

# Pronunciation & Stress

Russian pronunciation centers on one rule: stress dramatically changes vowel sounds. Unstressed О sounds like "a", unstressed Е like "i". There is no rule for predicting stress — it must be memorized per word.

## Core Vocabulary

| Cyrillic | romanization | English |
|----------|--------------|---------|
| хорошо́ | khoroshó | good (stress on last О) |
| молоко́ | molokó | milk (stress on last О) |
| спаси́бо | spasíbo | thank you |
| пожа́луйста | pozhálusta | please / you're welcome |
| здра́вствуйте | zdrástvuyte | hello (formal) |
| до свида́ния | do svidániya | goodbye |
| извини́те | izviníte | excuse me |
| да | da | yes |
| нет | net | no |
| сего́дня | sevódnya | today (Г pronounced V) |
| что | shto | what (Ч pronounced Sh) |
| коне́чно | konéshno | of course (Ч pronounced Sh) |

## Example Sentences

- **Здра́вствуйте!** (Zdrástvuyte!) — Hello! (the first В is silent)
- **Как дела́?** (Kak dilá?) — How are you? (unstressed Е → i)
- **Хорошо́, спаси́бо.** (Kharashó, spasíba.) — Fine, thanks. (unstressed О → a)
- **Что э́то?** (Shto éta?) — What is this?
- **Сего́дня хо́лодно.** (Sivódnya khóladna.) — Today it's cold.

## Pronunciation Rules

- **Vowel reduction (akanye)**: Unstressed О is pronounced "a". молоко́ → "ma-la-KO".
- **Ikanye**: Unstressed Е and Я reduce to "i". десять → "DYE-sit'".
- **Final devoicing**: B, Г, Д, Ж, З at the end of a word lose their voice. хлеб (khleb) → "khlep".
- **Г → В in genitive endings**: его́ → "yeVO", сего́дня → "siVODnya".
- **Ч → Ш in a few words**: что → "shto", коне́чно → "kanéshna".
- **Stress is unpredictable** and shifts under inflection: го́род (city) → города́ (cities).

## Common Mistakes

- Pronouncing every О as "o" — most are reduced to "a".
- Stressing the wrong syllable (often the first by default in English).
- Voicing final consonants. хлеб ends in "p", not "b".
- Forgetting that "что" sounds like "shto".

## Try It Yourself

1. Say "молоко" three times, stressing the last syllable: ma-la-KO.
2. Read: хорошо, спасибо, до свидания — mark stress.
3. Practice the silent В in здравствуйте.
4. Record yourself saying "Что это?" — make Ч sound like "sh".

## Next Steps

Now that you can sound out written Russian, learn essential greetings and survival phrases for real interactions.

# Greetings & Essential Phrases

Russian distinguishes formal (вы) from informal (ты) speech. Use formal forms with strangers, elders, and in business; informal with friends, family, and children.

## Core Vocabulary

| Cyrillic | romanization | English |
|----------|--------------|---------|
| Здра́вствуйте | Zdrávstvuyte | Hello (formal) |
| Приве́т | Privét | Hi (informal) |
| До свида́ния | Do svidániya | Goodbye |
| Пока́ | Paká | Bye (informal) |
| Спаси́бо | Spasíbo | Thank you |
| Пожа́луйста | Pozhálusta | Please / You're welcome |
| Извини́те | Izviníte | Excuse me / Sorry (formal) |
| Прости́те | Prostíte | I'm sorry (formal) |
| Да | Da | Yes |
| Нет | Net | No |
| Как дела́? | Kak delá? | How are you? |
| Хорошо́ | Khoroshó | Good / fine |
| Пло́хо | Plókha | Bad |
| Норма́льно | Normálʹno | OK, fine |
| Меня́ зову́т… | Menyá zovút… | My name is… |
| О́чень прия́тно | Óchenʹ priyátno | Nice to meet you |
| Я не понима́ю | Ya ne ponimáyu | I don't understand |
| Говори́те по-англи́йски? | Govoríte po-anglíyski? | Do you speak English? |

## Example Sentences

- **Здра́вствуйте, как ва́ши дела́?** (Zdrávstvuyte, kak váshi delá?) — Hello, how are you? (formal)
- **Приве́т! Как дела́?** (Privét! Kak delá?) — Hi! How are you? (informal)
- **Меня́ зову́т Áнна. А вас?** (Menyá zovút Ánna. A vas?) — My name is Anna. And yours?
- **Извини́те, я не понима́ю.** (Izviníte, ya ne ponimáyu.) — Excuse me, I don't understand.
- **Спаси́бо большо́е!** (Spasíbo bolʹshóye!) — Thank you very much!
- **До свида́ния, до за́втра.** (Do svidániya, do závtra.) — Goodbye, see you tomorrow.

## Grammar Notes

- **ты vs вы**: ты = singular informal; вы = plural OR singular formal. When in doubt, use вы.
- **No "is"**: Russian present-tense "to be" is omitted. "I am Anna" → Я Áнна.
- **Меня зовут** literally means "they call me" — there's no possessive "my" here.
- **Greetings change by time**: Доброе утро (good morning), Добрый день (good day), Добрый вечер (good evening).

## Common Mistakes

- Using ты with a stranger — feels rude. Default to вы.
- Saying "Я есть Анна" — incorrect; drop "to be".
- Translating "please" and "you're welcome" as different words — both are пожалуйста.

## Try It Yourself

1. Greet a teacher (formal) and a friend (informal).
2. Introduce yourself: Меня зову́т [your name].
3. Ask "How are you?" two ways and answer "Хорошо́, спаси́бо."
4. Apologize and say you don't understand.

## Next Steps

You can now open a conversation. Next: nouns, gender, and adjective agreement — the foundation of Russian grammar.

# Gender, Nouns & Adjective Agreement

Every Russian noun has one of three genders: masculine, feminine, or neuter. Adjectives, past-tense verbs, and pronouns must agree. Gender is usually predictable from the noun's ending.

## Core Vocabulary

| Cyrillic | romanization | English |
|----------|--------------|---------|
| стол | stol | table (masc.) |
| дом | dom | house (masc.) |
| студе́нт | studént | (male) student (masc.) |
| кни́га | kníga | book (fem.) |
| ма́ма | máma | mom (fem.) |
| студе́нтка | studéntka | (female) student (fem.) |
| окно́ | oknó | window (neut.) |
| мо́ре | móre | sea (neut.) |
| но́вый | nóvy | new (masc.) |
| но́вая | nóvaya | new (fem.) |
| но́вое | nóvoye | new (neut.) |
| хоро́ший | khoróshiy | good (masc.) |
| хоро́шая | khoróshaya | good (fem.) |
| хоро́шее | khoróshee | good (neut.) |
| большо́й | bolʹshóy | big (masc., stressed ending) |
| ма́ленький | málenʹkiy | small (masc.) |

## Example Sentences

- **Э́то но́вый дом.** (Éto nóvy dom.) — This is a new house.
- **Э́то но́вая кни́га.** (Éto nóvaya kníga.) — This is a new book.
- **Э́то но́вое окно́.** (Éto nóvoye oknó.) — This is a new window.
- **Большо́й стол и ма́ленький стул.** (Bolʹshóy stol i málenʹkiy stul.) — Big table and small chair.
- **Хоро́шая студе́нтка.** (Khoróshaya studéntka.) — A good (female) student.

## Grammar Notes

- **Masculine**: ends in a consonant (стол, дом) or -й (музе́й).
- **Feminine**: ends in -а / -я (кни́га, неде́ля).
- **Neuter**: ends in -о / -е (окно́, мо́ре).
- **-ь endings** are tricky: дверь (door) is feminine, день (day) is masculine — must be memorized.
- Adjectives agree in gender (and later in number and case). The dictionary form is masculine: -ый/-ий/-ой.
- Stressed adjective ending? Use -ой (большо́й). Unstressed? -ый (но́вый).

## Common Mistakes

- Assuming -а always = feminine: па́па and де́душка are masculine despite -а endings (refer to people).
- Forgetting to change adjective endings: "но́вый кни́га" is wrong — should be но́вая кни́га.
- Treating -ь nouns as one gender — half are masculine, half feminine.

## Try It Yourself

1. Identify gender: маши́на, телефо́н, письмо́, ночь.
2. Add "new" to each: маши́на → но́вая маши́на.
3. Translate: "a small house," "a good book," "a big sea."
4. List five masculine, five feminine, and five neuter nouns from this lesson.

## Next Steps

Adjectives also agree in case and number. First, learn how verbs conjugate in the present tense.

# Present Tense Conjugation

Russian verbs conjugate by person (1st, 2nd, 3rd) and number (singular, plural). There are two conjugation patterns: the -е- type (1st conjugation) and the -и- type (2nd conjugation).

## Core Vocabulary

| Cyrillic | romanization | English |
|----------|--------------|---------|
| чита́ть | chitátʹ | to read |
| писа́ть | pisátʹ | to write |
| рабо́тать | rabótatʹ | to work |
| жить | zhitʹ | to live |
| знать | znatʹ | to know |
| понима́ть | ponimátʹ | to understand |
| говори́ть | govorítʹ | to speak |
| ви́деть | vídetʹ | to see |
| слы́шать | slýshatʹ | to hear |
| люби́ть | lyubítʹ | to love |
| хоте́ть | khotétʹ | to want (irregular) |
| мочь | mochʹ | can / be able (irregular) |

## Example Sentences

- **Я чита́ю кни́гу.** (Ya chitáyu knígu.) — I read a book.
- **Ты говори́шь по-ру́сски?** (Ty govorishʹ po-rússki?) — Do you speak Russian?
- **Он живёт в Москве́.** (On zhivyót v Moskvé.) — He lives in Moscow.
- **Мы понима́ем все.** (My ponimáyem vsyo.) — We understand everything.
- **Они́ рабо́тают здесь.** (Oní rabótayut zdesʹ.) — They work here.
- **Я хочу́ ко́фе.** (Ya khochú kófe.) — I want coffee.

## Conjugation Patterns

### 1st conjugation (-е-): чита́ть (to read)
- я чита́ю (I read)
- ты чита́ешь (you read)
- он/она́ чита́ет (he/she reads)
- мы чита́ем (we read)
- вы чита́ете (you read, formal/plural)
- они́ чита́ют (they read)

### 2nd conjugation (-и-): говори́ть (to speak)
- я говорю́
- ты говори́шь
- он/она́ говори́т
- мы говори́м
- вы говори́те
- они́ говоря́т

## Grammar Notes

- The infinitive usually ends in -ть.
- Drop the -ть, add the personal ending.
- 1st conjugation has -ешь, -ет, -ем, -ете, -ют endings; 2nd has -ишь, -ит, -им, -ите, -ат/ят.
- Subject pronouns (я, ты, он) are usually included for clarity.
- Russian has only one present tense — there's no "I am reading" vs "I read" distinction.

## Common Mistakes

- Mixing the two conjugations: говори́ет (wrong) → говори́т.
- Forgetting stress shift: я пишу́, ты пи́шешь.
- Treating люби́ть as 1st conjugation — it's 2nd, with я люблю́ (mutation in 1st-person sg).

## Try It Yourself

1. Conjugate знать and ви́деть in all six forms.
2. Translate: "We work in Moscow," "She reads a book," "Do you (formal) understand?"
3. Make three sentences using я, ты, and они́.

## Next Steps

You can now form simple sentences. Next: cases. The nominative names the subject; the accusative marks the direct object.

# Nominative & Accusative Cases

Russian uses six grammatical cases. The nominative is the dictionary form (subject of the sentence). The accusative marks the direct object — what is being read, seen, bought.

## Core Vocabulary

| Cyrillic | romanization | English |
|----------|--------------|---------|
| кни́га → кни́гу | kníga → knígu | book (nom. → acc.) |
| газе́та → газе́ту | gazéta → gazétu | newspaper |
| маши́на → маши́ну | mashína → mashínu | car |
| ма́ма → ма́му | máma → mámu | mom |
| студе́нт → студе́нта | studént → studénta | (male) student |
| брат → бра́та | brat → bráta | brother |
| дом → дом | dom → dom | house (inanimate masc., no change) |
| окно́ → окно́ | oknó → oknó | window (neuter, no change) |
| меня́ | menyá | me (acc.) |
| тебя́ | tebyá | you (acc., informal) |
| его́ | yevó | him / it |
| её | yeyó | her |
| нас | nas | us |
| вас | vas | you (acc., formal/pl.) |
| их | ikh | them |

## Example Sentences

- **Я чита́ю кни́гу.** (Ya chitáyu knígu.) — I'm reading a book. (book = direct object → acc.)
- **Я люблю́ ма́му.** (Ya lyublyú mámu.) — I love mom.
- **Он ви́дит студе́нта.** (On vídit studénta.) — He sees the student. (animate masc. → -а)
- **Мы покупа́ем дом.** (My pokupáyem dom.) — We're buying a house. (inanim. masc. unchanged)
- **Она́ зна́ет меня́.** (Oná znáyet menyá.) — She knows me.
- **Я понима́ю вас.** (Ya ponimáyu vas.) — I understand you (formal).

## Case Rules

### Accusative endings
- **Feminine -а / -я** → -у / -ю: кни́га → кни́гу.
- **Masculine animate** (people, animals) → add -а / -я: брат → бра́та.
- **Masculine inanimate** → no change: стол → стол.
- **Neuter** → no change: окно́ → окно́.
- **Plural animate** → genitive form (advanced).
- **Plural inanimate** → same as nominative.

## Grammar Notes

- The accusative answers "Кого́?" (whom?) for animate and "Что?" (what?) for inanimate.
- Animacy matters only in the masculine singular and all plurals.
- After verbs of motion + в/на, use accusative for direction: е́ду в Москву́ (going to Moscow).

## Common Mistakes

- Treating all masculine nouns the same — animacy determines accusative form.
- Forgetting feminine -у ending: "Я чита́ю кни́га" is wrong → кни́гу.
- Mixing меня́ (acc./gen.) with мне (dat.).

## Try It Yourself

1. Put into accusative: газе́та, бра́т, ма́ма, дом, окно́.
2. Translate: "I see her," "We know him," "She buys a newspaper."
3. Write three sentences with accusative direct objects.

## Next Steps

Two cases down, four to go. Before tackling more cases, build vocabulary: numbers, time, family, food, and city life.

# Numbers, Time & Calendar

Russian numbers trigger different cases: 1 takes nominative, 2-4 take genitive singular, 5+ take genitive plural. Time and dates use specific case patterns you can memorize as chunks.

## Core Vocabulary

| Cyrillic | romanization | English |
|----------|--------------|---------|
| оди́н / одна́ / одно́ | odín / odná / odnó | one (m/f/n) |
| два / две | dva / dve | two (m,n / f) |
| три | tri | three |
| четы́ре | chetýre | four |
| пять | pyatʹ | five |
| де́сять | désyatʹ | ten |
| два́дцать | dvádtsatʹ | twenty |
| сто | sto | one hundred |
| ты́сяча | týsyacha | one thousand |
| понеде́льник | ponedélʹnik | Monday |
| вто́рник | vtórnik | Tuesday |
| среда́ | sredá | Wednesday |
| четве́рг | chetvérg | Thursday |
| пя́тница | pyátnitsa | Friday |
| суббо́та | subbóta | Saturday |
| воскресе́нье | voskresénʹye | Sunday |
| янва́рь | yanvárʹ | January |
| фе́враль | fevrálʹ | February |
| год | god | year |
| ме́сяц | mésyats | month |
| неде́ля | nedélya | week |
| день | denʹ | day |
| час | chas | hour |
| мину́та | minúta | minute |
| сейча́с | seychás | now |
| вчера́ | vcherá | yesterday |
| сего́дня | sevódnya | today |
| за́втра | závtra | tomorrow |

## Example Sentences

- **Сейча́с три часа́.** (Seychás tri chasá.) — It's three o'clock. (3 + gen. sg.)
- **Сейча́с пять часо́в.** (Seychás pyatʹ chasóv.) — It's five o'clock. (5 + gen. pl.)
- **В понеде́льник я рабо́таю.** (V ponedélʹnik ya rabótayu.) — On Monday I work.
- **Сего́дня среда́.** (Sevódnya sredá.) — Today is Wednesday.
- **Мне два́дцать лет.** (Mne dvádtsatʹ let.) — I'm twenty years old. (lit. "to me twenty years")
- **В январе́ хо́лодно.** (V yanvaré khóladna.) — In January it's cold.

## Grammar Notes

- After 1 (and any number ending in 1, except 11): nominative singular. оди́н дом.
- After 2, 3, 4 (and 22, 23, 24…): genitive singular. два до́ма.
- After 5-20 (and 25-30, then 35+): genitive plural. пять домо́в.
- Days of the week: use **в + accusative**: в понеде́льник, в суббо́ту.
- Months: use **в + prepositional**: в январе́, в ма́е.
- Age: dative + год / го́да / лет. Мне 1 год, 2 го́да, 5 лет.

## Common Mistakes

- Saying "пять часа́" — should be пять часо́в.
- Confusing год / го́да / лет (singular / 2-4 / 5+).
- Forgetting в + accusative for weekdays.

## Try It Yourself

1. Count to 10 in Russian.
2. Say what day it is today and tomorrow.
3. State your age: "Мне ___ лет / го́да."
4. Translate: "It's two o'clock," "On Friday I'm free," "In May it's warm."

## Next Steps

You can tell time and date. Next: family, food, and home — the core of daily-life vocabulary.

# Family, Food & Home

Daily-life vocabulary is the fastest path to real conversation. Russian food and family terms also introduce diminutives (-очка, -ик), which are everywhere in spoken Russian.

| мать / ма́ма | matʹ / máma | mother / mom |

| сын | syn | son |
| дочь | dochʹ | daughter |
| ба́бушка | bábushka | grandmother |
| де́душка | dédushka | grandfather |
| муж | muzh | husband |
| жена́ | zhená | wife |
| хлеб | khleb | bread |
| вода́ | vodá | water |
| ча́й | chay | tea |
| ко́фе | kófe | coffee |
| молоко́ | molokó | milk |

| дом | dom | house |
| кварти́ра | kvartíra | apartment |
| ко́мната | kómnata | room |
| ку́хня | kúkhnya | kitchen |
| ва́нная | vánnaya | bathroom |
| окно́ | oknó | window |
| дверь | dverʹ | door |

## Example Sentences

- **У меня́ есть брат и сестра́.** (U menyá yestʹ brat i sestrá.) — I have a brother and sister.
- **Моя́ ма́ма — врач.** (Moyá máma — vrach.) — My mom is a doctor.
- **Я люблю́ ко́фе с молоко́м.** (Ya lyublyú kófe s molokóm.) — I love coffee with milk.
- **На обе́д у нас борщ.** (Na obéd u nas borshch.) — For lunch we have borscht.
- **На́ша кварти́ра ма́ленькая, но ую́тная.** (Násha kvartíra málenʹkaya, no uyútnaya.) — Our apartment is small but cozy.
- **В ку́хне есть стол и стул.** (V kúkhne yestʹ stol i stul.) — In the kitchen there's a table and chair.

## Grammar Notes

- "To have" is expressed with **У + genitive + есть**: У меня́ есть кни́га = I have a book.
- Possessives agree in gender: мой брат / моя́ сестра́ / моё окно́.
- Diminutives soften and warm: ма́ма → ма́мочка, кни́га → кни́жка, дом → до́мик.
- Russian has no articles ("a/the"). Context determines definiteness.

## Common Mistakes

- Saying "Я име́ю кни́гу" — grammatically possible but unnatural. Use У меня́ есть.
- Mixing моя́ / мой / моё — must match noun gender.
- Forgetting that дочь and мать stay declension-irregular (дочь → до́чери in genitive).

## Try It Yourself

1. Describe your family: У меня́ есть… .
2. Order breakfast: ко́фе, хлеб, сыр.
3. Describe your home in 3 sentences.
4. Use a diminutive: ма́мочка, ко́тик, до́мик.

## Next Steps

You can talk about home and family. Next: leaving the house — city, transport, and shopping.

Getting around Russian cities means metro, marshrutka (minibus), and tram. Shopping introduces the genitive case for "no", quantities, and prices.

| у́лица | úlitsa | street |

| маши́на | mashína | car |

| остано́вка | ostanóvka | bus stop |

| ры́нок | rýnok | market |
| апте́ка | aptéka | pharmacy |
| банк | bank | bank |
| рестора́н | restorán | restaurant |
| рубль | rublʹ | ruble |
| де́ньги | dénʹgi | money |
| ско́лько | skólʹko | how much / how many |
| где | gde | where |
| как | kak | how |
| напра́во | naprávo | to the right |
| нале́во | naléva | to the left |
| пря́мо | pryámo | straight ahead |

## Example Sentences

- **Где метро́?** (Gde metró?) — Where's the metro?
- **Иди́те пря́мо, пото́м напра́во.** (Idíte pryámo, potóm naprávo.) — Go straight, then right.
- **Ско́лько сто́ит биле́т?** (Skólʹko stóit bilét?) — How much is the ticket?
- **Сто рубле́й.** (Sto rubléy.) — One hundred rubles.
- **Я е́ду на авто́бусе.** (Ya yédu na avtóbuse.) — I'm going by bus.
- **В магази́не нет хле́ба.** (V magazíne net khléba.) — There's no bread in the store.

## Grammar Notes

- **By transport**: на + prepositional. на метро́, на авто́бусе, на маши́не.
- **To a place**: в / на + accusative. в магази́н, на рабо́ту.
- **At a place**: в / на + prepositional. в магази́не, на рабо́те.
- **Negation "no/none"**: нет + genitive. У меня́ нет вре́мени = I have no time.
- **Prices**: 1 рубль, 2-4 рубля́, 5+ рубле́й.

## Common Mistakes

- Saying "в авто́бус" for "by bus" — should be на авто́бусе (location-style).
- Forgetting genitive after нет: "нет хлеб" → нет хле́ба.
- Confusing идти́ (go on foot) with е́хать (go by vehicle).

## Try It Yourself

1. Ask "Where is the bank?" / "How much is coffee?"
2. Give directions: straight, then left, then right.
3. Say "I'm going to work by metro."

# Introductions & Polite Speech

Russian formal speech uses вы and full first name + patronymic (e.g., Ива́н Петро́вич). Knowing when to switch to ты is a cultural skill — usually when invited.

## Core Vocabulary

| Cyrillic | romanization | English |
|----------|--------------|---------|
| Разреши́те предста́виться | Razreshíte predstávitʹsya | Allow me to introduce myself |
| Меня́ зову́т… | Menyá zovút… | My name is… |
| Я из… | Ya iz… | I'm from… |
| О́чень прия́тно | Óchenʹ priyátno | Pleased to meet you |
| Как вас зову́т? | Kak vas zovút? | What's your name? (formal) |
| Как тебя́ зову́т? | Kak tebyá zovút? | What's your name? (informal) |
| Кто вы по профе́ссии? | Kto vy po proféssii? | What's your profession? |
| Я студе́нт / студе́нтка | Ya studént / studéntka | I'm a (m/f) student |
| Я инжене́р | Ya inzhenér | I'm an engineer |
| Я врач | Ya vrach | I'm a doctor |
| Я учи́тель | Ya uchítelʹ | I'm a teacher |
| Где вы живёте? | Gde vy zhivyóte? | Where do you live? |
| Я живу́ в… | Ya zhivú v… | I live in… |
| Ско́лько вам лет? | Skólʹko vam let? | How old are you? (formal) |
| Мне… лет | Mne… let | I'm… years old |
| господи́н / госпожа́ | gospodín / gospozhá | Mr. / Ms. |

## Example Sentences

- **Здра́вствуйте! Меня́ зову́т Ива́н Петро́вич Смирно́в.** (Zdrávstvuyte! Menyá zovút Iván Petróvich Smirnóv.) — Hello! My name is Ivan Petrovich Smirnov.
- **О́чень прия́тно, я Áнна.** (Óchenʹ priyátno, ya Ánna.) — Pleased to meet you, I'm Anna.
- **Я из Аме́рики, из Нью-Йо́рка.** (Ya iz Amériki, iz Nʹyu-Yórka.) — I'm from America, from New York.
- **Кем вы рабо́таете?** (Kem vy rabótayete?) — What do you do for work?
- **Я рабо́таю программи́стом.** (Ya rabótayu programmístom.) — I work as a programmer. (instr. case)
- **Дава́йте на ты.** (Davayte na ty.) — Let's switch to "ты."

## Grammar Notes

- **из + genitive** for origin: из Аме́рики, из Москвы́.
- **в + prepositional** for residence: в Москве́, в Нью-Йо́рке.
- **рабо́тать + instrumental** for profession: рабо́таю учи́телем (I work as a teacher).
- **Patronymic**: middle name from father's name + -ович (m) / -овна (f). Used in formal address.
- **Дава́йте на ты** is the polite request to drop formality.

## Common Mistakes

- Using ты with someone older or in business — stick to вы.
- Saying "Я есть студе́нт" — drop "to be": Я студе́нт.
- Translating profession with nominative ("Я программи́ст") works, but instrumental + рабо́тать is more idiomatic for "I work as…".

## Try It Yourself

1. Introduce yourself formally: name, origin, profession, age.
2. Ask a stranger their name and where they're from.
3. Switch from вы to ты in role-play.
4. Practice patronymic with a Russian name.

## Next Steps

Polite speech in social settings. Now navigate restaurants and hotels.

## Example Sentences

- **Вход с у́лицы Тверска́я.** (Vkhod s úlitsy Tverskáya.) — Entrance from Tverskaya Street.
- **Магази́н откры́т с 9:00 до 21:00.** (Magazín otkrýt s 9:00 do 21:00.) — Store open from 9 to 9.
- **Распрода́жа: ски́дка 50%.** (Rasprodázha: skídka 50%.) — Sale: 50% off.
- **Внима́ние! Двери́ закрыва́ются.** (Vnimániye! Dveri zakryváyutsya.) — Attention! Doors closing.
- **Заголо́вок газе́ты: «Экономи́ческий кри́зис».** (…) — Newspaper headline: "Economic Crisis."

## Reading Strategies

- **Spot cognates**: информа́ция, рестора́н, телефо́н, университе́т — many Russian words borrow Greek/Latin/French roots.
- **Recognize prefixes**: за- (closed off), вы- (out), при- (toward), от- (away). закры́то = "closed off."
- **Endings betray case**: -е / -ой / -ом are usually prep. or instr. — context tells you.
- **Read aloud**: Russian is mostly phonetic; you can decode unfamiliar words.

- Skipping unknown words — learn to extract case/role first, look up later.
- Translating cognates as their English meaning blindly: симпати́чный = "nice-looking", not "sympathetic."

| дорого́й / дорога́я | dorogóy / dorogáya | dear (m / f) |
| при́выв | privét | hi (informal opening) |
| уважа́емый | uvazháyemyy | respected (formal opening) |

## Example Sentences

- **Дорога́я Áнна, как у тебя́ дела́?** (Dorogáya Ánna, kak u tebyá delá?) — Dear Anna, how are you?
- **Уважа́емый господи́н Ивано́в!** (Uvazháyemyy gospodín Ivanóv!) — Respected Mr. Ivanov! (formal letter opening)
- **Я пишу́ тебе́ из Москвы́.** (Ya pishú tebé iz Moskvý.) — I'm writing to you from Moscow.
- **С уваже́нием, Сергéй.** (S uvazhéniyem, Sergéy.) — Sincerely, Sergei.
- **— Приве́т! — сказа́ла Ма́ша.** (— Privét! — skazála Másha.) — "Hi!" said Masha. (dialogue dash)

## Writing Notes

- **Cursive is mandatory** in Russian schools and shapes differ from print: т looks like an English "m," д like a "g," and в has a loop.
- **Quotation marks**: Russian uses «guillemets» for quotes. «Война и мир».
- **Dialogue uses em-dashes**, not quotation marks.
- **Comma rules** are strict — Russian commas appear before subordinate clauses (что, который, потому что).
- **Address format**: Country → city → street → building/apartment → name (reverse of US).

## Common Mistakes

- Writing print Cyrillic where cursive is expected.
- Forgetting comma before что: "Я ду́маю что…" → Я ду́маю, что…
- Using English "smart quotes" instead of «guillemets».

3. Write a formal email to a teacher with proper opening and sign-off.

## Core Vocabulary

## Example Excerpts

- **«Все счастли́вые се́мьи похо́жи друг на дру́га, ка́ждая несчастли́вая семья́ несчастли́ва по-сво́ему.»** — Лев Толсто́й, «Áнна Каре́нина». ("All happy families are alike; each unhappy family is unhappy in its own way." — Tolstoy.)
- **«Я вас люби́л: любо́вь ещё, быть мо́жет, в душе́ мое́й уга́сла не совсе́м…»** — А. С. Пу́шкин. ("I loved you: love perhaps has not yet quite died out in my soul…" — Pushkin.)
- **«Краси́вость спасёт мир.»** — Ф. М. Достое́вский, «Идио́т». (Often translated "Beauty will save the world.")
- **«В Москве́ есть дворы́, в кото́рых ни́когда не быва́ет со́лнца.»** — Ан. Чехов. (Free: "In Moscow there are courtyards where the sun never reaches.")

## Reading Notes

- **19th-century Russian** uses some archaic forms (e.g., -ыя endings, ять letter Ѣ in pre-1918 spelling).
- **Word order is flexible** for emphasis: poets often invert subject/verb.
- **Pushkin's iambic tetrameter** in *Eugene Onegin* is the gold standard of Russian verse.
- **Chekhov's prose** is famously concise — every word counts.

## Common Mistakes

- Expecting modern grammar from 19th-century texts.
- Trying to read Tolstoy linearly without skimming — sentences run long.
- Ignoring stress marks in poetry — they cue meter.

1. Memorize one Pushkin couplet.
2. Read aloud Tolstoy's first line of *Anna Karenina*.
3. Find a Chekhov micro-story and identify three new vocabulary items.
4. Compare a passage in Russian and English translation.

| тост | tost | toast (drinking) |
| ба́ня | bánya | Russian sauna |
| дача | dácha | summer cottage |

## Example Sentences

- **С Но́вым го́дом!** (S Nóvym gódom!) — Happy New Year!
- **С пра́здником!** (S prázdnikom!) — Happy holiday! (universal)
- **На Ма́сленицу мы пе́чём блины́.** (Na Máslenitsu my pechyóm bliný.) — On Maslenitsa we bake blini.
- **С 8 Ма́рта!** (S vosʹmým mártom!) — Happy March 8th!
- **9 Ма́я мы вспомина́ем побе́ду.** (Devyátogo máya my vspomináyem pobédu.) — On May 9th we remember the victory.
- **Пое́дем на да́чу на выходны́е.** (Poyédem na dáchu na vykhodnýye.) — Let's go to the dacha for the weekend.

## Cultural Notes

- **New Year, not Christmas, is the biggest holiday.** Soviet atheism shifted Christmas customs (tree, gifts, Father Frost) to Dec 31.
- **Orthodox Christmas** falls on Jan 7 because the Russian Church follows the Julian calendar.
- **Maslenitsa**: a week of pancakes before Lent, ending with burning a straw effigy of winter.
- **Victory Day (May 9)**: extremely solemn, commemorating WWII; "Immortal Regiment" marches feature photos of fallen relatives.
- **Toasts** are mandatory at meals — usually three minimum, ending with one to women.

## Common Mistakes

- Wishing "Merry Christmas" on Dec 25 — Russians celebrate Jan 7.
- Treating 8 Марта as casual — it's a major day, give flowers.
- Confusing Дед Мороз with Santa: he wears blue or red, walks with Снегурочка, and arrives on Dec 31.

2. Describe Maslenitsa in 3 sentences.

# All Six Cases

Russian has six cases: nominative, accusative, genitive, dative, instrumental, prepositional. Each marks a different role for the noun. Mastering them is the single biggest step toward fluency.

## Quick Reference (feminine -а noun: кни́га)

| Case | Form | Function | Example |
|------|------|----------|---------|
| Nominative | кни́га | subject | Кни́га на столе́. |
| Accusative | кни́гу | direct object | Я чита́ю кни́гу. |
| Genitive | кни́ги | possession, "of", negation | Стра́ница кни́ги. У меня́ нет кни́ги. |
| Dative | кни́ге | indirect object, recipient | Я дам кни́ге… (rare for objects); Мне нра́вится кни́га. |
| Instrumental | кни́гой | "by/with" instrument | Я гото́влю с кни́гой. |
| Prepositional | (о) кни́ге | location, "about" | О кни́ге. В кни́ге. |

## Trigger Prepositions

- **в, на + accusative**: motion (to). в Москву́.
- **в, на + prepositional**: location (in/at). в Москве́.
- **из, с, до, у, без, для, около, после + genitive**: из Москвы́, для тебя́, без са́хара.
- **к + dative**: motion toward a person. к врачу́.
- **с, над, под, перед, между + instrumental**: с дру́гом, под столо́м.
- **о, об + prepositional**: about. о любви́.

## Example Sentences

- **(Nom.) Маши́на стои́т.** — The car is standing.
- **(Acc.) Я ви́жу маши́ну.** — I see the car.
- **(Gen.) Цвет маши́ны — кра́сный.** — The car's color is red.
- **(Dat.) Маши́не нужны́ ши́ны.** — The car needs tires.
- **(Instr.) Я е́ду маши́ной.** — I go by car.
- **(Prep.) Мы говори́м о маши́не.** — We're talking about the car.

## Grammar Notes

- Each noun has 12 possible forms (6 cases × 2 numbers).
- Three declension types for nouns; adjectives follow their own pattern.
- Memorize **case + preposition** as a chunk: "о + prep.", "из + gen.", "к + dat."
- Pronouns decline too: я / меня́ / меня́ / мне / мной / (обо) мне.

## Common Mistakes

- Using accusative after о — should be prepositional. о кни́ге, not о кни́гу.
- Forgetting that motion toward a person uses к + dative (к ма́ме), not в.
- Mixing genitive of negation: "У меня́ нет кни́га" → нет кни́ги.

## Try It Yourself

1. Decline стол in all 6 cases (singular).
2. Decline кни́га, ма́ма, окно́.
3. Translate: "I'm going to my friend (к + dat.)," "I'm thinking about you (о + prep.)," "without water (без + gen.)."
4. Pick a paragraph from any Russian text and identify each case.

## Next Steps

Cases handle "who/what." Next: how Russian expresses "completed vs ongoing" — verbal aspect.

# Verbal Aspect: Perfective & Imperfective

Russian has two aspects, not three tenses. Almost every verb has an imperfective partner (ongoing/repeated/general) and a perfective partner (completed/single/result-focused).

## Core Vocabulary (aspect pairs)

| Imperfective | Perfective | English |
|--------------|------------|---------|
| де́лать | сде́лать | to do / to do (and finish) |
| писа́ть | написа́ть | to write |
| чита́ть | прочита́ть | to read |
| смотре́ть | посмотре́ть | to watch |
| есть | съесть | to eat |
| пить | вы́пить | to drink |
| понима́ть | поня́ть | to understand |
| говори́ть | сказа́ть | to speak / to say |
| брать | взять | to take |
| дава́ть | дать | to give |
| покупа́ть | купи́ть | to buy |
| вспомина́ть | вспо́мнить | to remember |

## Example Sentences

- **Я чита́л кни́гу два часа́.** (Imp.) — I was reading a book for two hours. (process)
- **Я прочита́л кни́гу.** (Pf.) — I read the book (finished it).
- **Что ты де́лал вчера́?** (Imp.) — What were you doing yesterday?
- **Я сде́лал дома́шнее зада́ние.** (Pf.) — I did (finished) the homework.
- **Я пишу́ письмо́.** (Imp., now) — I'm writing a letter.
- **Я напишу́ письмо́ за́втра.** (Pf., future) — I'll write (and finish) a letter tomorrow.

## Grammar Notes

- **Imperfective** describes the process, repeated actions, or general statements.
- **Perfective** describes a single completed action with a result.
- **Perfective has no present tense** — its conjugated form is always future. Я напишу́ = "I will write."
- Future tense:
  - Imperfective: бу́ду + infinitive (бу́ду чита́ть = will be reading).
  - Perfective: conjugated form of perfective verb (прочита́ю = will have read).
- Pairs are formed by prefix (на-, про-, с-) or stem change.

## Common Mistakes

- Treating perfective as past-only — it forms the future too.
- Saying "Я бу́ду прочита́ть" — wrong. Use бу́ду only with imperfective.
- Choosing imperfective for one-time completed events: "Я чита́л кни́гу" implies process; for "I read this book once," use Я прочита́л.

## Try It Yourself

1. List 5 aspect pairs and their meanings.
2. Translate using the right aspect: "I wrote two letters yesterday" (Pf.); "I write every day" (Imp.).
3. Build the future tense for both aspects of писа́ть.
4. Choose: ел/съел? "I ate the whole cake" → съел.

## Next Steps

Aspect masters time. Next: motion verbs — Russia's notorious "go" system.

# Verbs of Motion

Russian has multiple verbs for "to go," distinguished by direction (one-way vs round-trip), means (foot vs vehicle), and aspect. Adding prefixes (при-, у-, в-, вы-, до-) creates dozens more.

## Core Vocabulary

| Imperfective unidirectional | Imperfective multi-directional | Meaning |
|------|------|---------|
| идти́ | ходи́ть | to go on foot |
| е́хать | е́здить | to go by vehicle |
| лете́ть | лета́ть | to fly |
| плыть | пла́вать | to swim / sail |
| бежа́ть | бе́гать | to run |
| нести́ | носи́ть | to carry |
| везти́ | вози́ть | to transport |
| вести́ | води́ть | to lead |

## Example Sentences

- **Я иду́ в магази́н.** (Ya idú v magazín.) — I'm going (now, on foot, one-way) to the store.
- **Я хожу́ в магази́н ка́ждый день.** (Ya khozhú v magazín kázhdyy denʹ.) — I go to the store every day. (habitual)
- **Я е́ду в Москву́.** (Ya yédu v Moskvú.) — I'm going (right now, by vehicle) to Moscow.
- **Я е́зжу в Москву́ ка́ждый ме́сяц.** (Ya yézzhu v Moskvú kázhdyy mésyats.) — I travel to Moscow every month.
- **Самолёт лети́т в Пари́ж.** (Samolyót letít v Parízh.) — The plane is flying to Paris.

## Common Prefixes (with идти́ → пойти́, прийти́…)

| Prefix | Meaning | Example |
|--------|---------|---------|
| по- | start going | пойти́ — to set off |
| при- | arrive | прийти́ — to come / arrive |
| у- | leave (away) | уйти́ — to leave |
| в- | enter | войти́ — to enter |
| вы- | exit | вы́йти — to exit |
| до- | reach | дойти́ — to reach |
| пере- | cross | перейти́ — to cross |

## Grammar Notes

- **Unidirectional** (идти́, е́хать): action in progress, one direction, one occurrence.
- **Multi-directional** (ходи́ть, е́здить): habitual, round-trip, ability.
- Prefix + unidirectional often becomes perfective: пойти́, прие́хать.
- Prefix + multi-directional stays imperfective: приходи́ть, приезжа́ть.

## Common Mistakes

- Using идти́ for habitual trips — should be ходи́ть.
- Using е́хать on foot — should be идти́.
- Forgetting that ходи́л can mean "I went and came back" (round-trip), while шёл means "I was on the way."

## Try It Yourself

1. Translate: "I go to school every day" (ходи́ть); "I'm going to school now" (идти́).
2. Translate: "He flew to Paris yesterday" (Pf., полете́л).
3. Build 3 prefix verbs from идти́: войти́, вы́йти, перейти́.
4. Use е́хать vs е́здить in two sentences.

## Next Steps

Motion verbs unlock travel narratives. Next: complex sentences and participles.

# Complex Sentences & Participles

Advanced Russian uses subordinate clauses (что, кото́рый, потому́ что), participles (verbal adjectives), and gerunds (verbal adverbs) to combine ideas in a single sentence.

## Core Vocabulary

| Cyrillic | romanization | English |
|----------|--------------|---------|
| что | shto | that (conj.) |
| кото́рый | kotóryy | which / who (relative) |
| потому́ что | potomú shto | because |
| е́сли | yésli | if |
| хотя́ | khotyá | although |
| когда́ | kogdá | when |
| пока́ | paká | while / until |
| что́бы | shtóby | in order to / so that |
| чита́ющий | chitáyushchiy | reading (act. part., pres.) |
| прочита́вший | prochitávshiy | (one who) read (act. part., past) |
| прочи́танный | prochítannyy | (something) read (pass. part., past) |
| чита́я | chitáya | while reading (gerund, imp.) |
| прочита́в | prochitáv | having read (gerund, pf.) |

## Example Sentences

- **Я зна́ю, что ты прав.** (Ya znáyu, shto ty prav.) — I know (that) you're right.
- **Челове́к, кото́рый говори́т по-ру́сски, мой друг.** (Chelovék, kotóryy govorít po-rússki, moy drug.) — The person who speaks Russian is my friend.
- **Я не пошёл, потому́ что был бо́лен.** (Ya ne poshyól, potomú shto byl bólen.) — I didn't go because I was sick.
- **Е́сли бу́дет дождь, мы оста́немся до́ма.** (Yésli búdet dozhdʹ, my ostánemsya dóma.) — If it rains, we'll stay home.
- **Я учу́, что́бы говори́ть лу́чше.** (Ya uchú, shtóby govorítʹ lúchshe.) — I study (so as) to speak better.
- **Прочита́в кни́гу, я лёг спать.** (Prochitáv knígu, ya lyog spatʹ.) — Having read the book, I went to sleep.

## Grammar Notes

- **Кото́рый** agrees with its antecedent in gender and number, but takes the case its role in the subordinate clause requires.
- **Что́бы** + infinitive (same subject) or **что́бы** + past tense (different subject).
- **Active participles** describe nouns: чита́ющий ма́льчик = "the reading boy."
- **Gerunds** modify the main verb: чита́я кни́гу, я слу́шал му́зыку = "while reading, I listened…".
- Always put a comma before subordinate conjunctions (что, что́бы, кото́рый, потому́ что).

## Common Mistakes

- Forgetting commas before что — Russian punctuation is strict.
- Using infinitive with что́бы when subjects differ — must use past-tense что́бы он пришёл, not что́бы прийти́.
- Mismatching кото́рый case to its antecedent.

## Try It Yourself

1. Combine: "I have a friend. He lives in Moscow." → using кото́рый.
2. Translate: "I study Russian so that I can read Tolstoy."
3. Form a participle: "the working man" → рабо́тающий челове́к.
4. Use a gerund: "Coming home, I called my mother."

## Next Steps

Complex grammar locked. Next: the colorful world of idioms and formal register.

# Idioms, Proverbs & Formal Register

Mastering Russian means moving between idiomatic colloquial speech and the dense formality of business or academic writing.

## Common Idioms

| Cyrillic | romanization | English / meaning |
|----------|--------------|-------------------|
| ни пу́ха ни пера́! | ni púkha ni perá! | "Neither fluff nor feather!" — good luck! (reply: к чёрту!) |
| де́ло в шля́пе | délo v shlyápe | "The deal is in the hat" — it's in the bag |
| кот в мешке́ | kot v meshké | "Cat in a bag" — pig in a poke |
| вили́лa бы́лa на воде́ | vílami po vodé | uncertain, "with a pitchfork on water" |
| води́ть за нос | vodítʹ za nos | to lead by the nose, to deceive |
| с гла́зу на глаз | s glázu na glaz | tête-à-tête, face to face |
| как ры́ба в воде́ | kak rýba v vodé | "like a fish in water" — at home, comfortable |
| ме́жду на́ми | mézhdu námi | between us |

## Common Proverbs

- **Ти́ше е́дешь — да́льше бу́дешь.** (Tíshe yédeshʹ — dálʹshe búdeshʹ.) — Slow and steady wins the race.
- **Без труда́ не вы́ловишь и ры́бку из пруда́.** — No pain, no gain.
- **Пе́рвый блин ко́мом.** — The first pancake is always a flop.
- **В чужо́й монасты́рь со свои́м уста́вом не хо́дят.** — When in Rome, do as the Romans do.
- **Слово́ не воробе́й, вы́летит — не пойма́ешь.** — A word, once spoken, can't be caught.

## Formal Register

| Informal | Formal | Note |
|----------|--------|------|
| ты | вы | always use вы in writing |
| Здра́сте | Здра́вствуйте | full greeting |
| окей | хорошо́ / согла́сен | OK → I agree |
| споко́йной но́чи | разреши́те откла́няться | take leave in formal speech |
| хочу́ | хоте́л(а) бы | I would like |
| мо́жно | разреши́те | may I |
| что́-то | не́что | something (formal/literary) |

## Example Sentences

- **Уважа́емые го́сти, разреши́те предста́вить…** — Distinguished guests, allow me to introduce…
- **В соотве́тствии с зако́ном…** — In accordance with the law…
- **Прошу́ вас обрати́ть внима́ние.** — I request you pay attention.
- **С глубо́ким уваже́нием.** — With deepest respect (sign-off).

## Common Mistakes

- Translating idioms literally — кот в мешке is not "cat in bag," it's risk in disguise.
- Mixing registers in one document — keep formal letters fully formal.
- Using ты-forms in business email.

## Try It Yourself

1. Memorize 5 idioms and use one in conversation.
2. Translate "first pancake's a flop" — and explain why pancakes.
3. Rewrite a casual sentence in formal register.
4. Sign a fake formal letter with «С глубоким уваже́нием».

# TORFL Exam Preparation

The TORFL (Тест по ру́сскому языку́ как иностра́нному, ТРКИ) certifies Russian proficiency on a 6-level scale: A1 (Elementary), A2 (Basic), B1 (First Certificate / TORFL-I), B2 (TORFL-II), C1 (TORFL-III), C2 (TORFL-IV).

## Exam Structure

Each TORFL level has five subtests:
1. **Чте́ние** (Reading) — texts with multiple-choice questions.
2. **Письмо́** (Writing) — letters, essays, summaries.
3. **Аудирова́ние** (Listening) — recorded dialogues, news, monologues.
4. **Говоре́ние** (Speaking) — guided dialogues + monologue tasks.
5. **Гра́мматика и ле́ксика** (Grammar & Vocabulary) — multiple choice.

To pass, you need ≥66% on each subtest.

## Core Vocabulary

| Cyrillic | romanization | English |
|----------|--------------|---------|
| экза́мен | ekzámen | exam |
| те́ст | test | test |
| у́ровень | úrovenʹ | level |
| сертифика́т | sertifikát | certificate |
| зада́ние | zadániye | task |
| балл | ball | point / score |
| сдать экза́мен | sdatʹ ekzámen | to pass an exam |
| провали́ть | provalítʹ | to fail |
| гото́виться к | gotóvitʹsya k | to prepare for |
| репети́тор | repetítor | tutor |
| образе́ц | obrazéts | sample / model |

## Level Targets

- **A1**: ~780 words; greetings, daily life, simple questions.
- **A2**: ~1,300 words; everyday topics, past tense.
- **B1 (TORFL-I)**: ~2,300 words; opinions, narratives, all six cases.
- **B2 (TORFL-II)**: ~6,000 words; abstract topics, idioms, complex syntax. Required for university study.
- **C1 (TORFL-III)**: ~12,000 words; near-native fluency, professional discourse.
- **C2 (TORFL-IV)**: native-level command, philological work.

## Strategy Tips

- **Time yourself**: each subtest has a strict time limit (usually 50-90 min).
- **Master the answer format**: TORFL uses specific multiple-choice and writing rubrics — practice with official samples.
- **Mock exam every 2 weeks**: build stamina; the test runs ~4-5 hours.
- **Speaking**: practice answering with full sentences. Avoid one-word replies.
- **Listening**: train with Russian podcasts at 1x then 1.25x speed.
- **Vocabulary**: drill the active list for your target level (lists are public).

## Example Sentences

- **Я гото́влюсь к экза́мену ТРКИ-2.** (Ya gotóvlyusʹ k ekzámenu TRKI-2.) — I'm preparing for the TORFL-II.
- **Я сдал экза́мен на 87 ба́ллов.** (Ya sdal ekzámen na vósemʹdesyat semʹ bállov.) — I passed the exam with 87 points.
- **На́до пройти́ ка́ждый разде́л.** (Nádo proytí kázhdyy razdél.) — You have to pass each section.

## Common Mistakes

- Skipping the writing subtest — students often underestimate it; practice formal letters and essays.
- Cramming vocabulary without context — TORFL tests collocations and case usage, not isolated words.
- Ignoring official sample tests — they reveal exact format quirks.

## Try It Yourself

1. Take a free A2 sample test online.
2. Write a 100-word essay: «Моя́ семья́».
3. Listen to a Russian news segment and summarize in 5 sentences.
4. Identify your target level and find an official sample.

## Next Steps

You have a complete Russian foundation: alphabet → cases → aspect → motion → register → exam-ready. From here, real fluency comes from sustained input — Russian books, podcasts, films, and conversations. Удачи!
